prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a tabletop workspace sloping away from the camera wearer, with the camera wearer's own hands in the bottom foreground at roughly 0.3 to 0.4 metres and a seated companion on the right side of the table about 0.5 to 0.8 metres away. On the tabletop to the left and behind the foreground workspace (roughly 0.7 to 1.1 metres from the camera wearer and 0.4 to 0.6 metres to the left of the companion), an upright cardboard box, plastic bags of toy blocks, and stacked boxes/books stand out as intermediate-gray structures against the dark background room (>2 metres away). Both the camera wearer's hands and the companion's two arms reach into the shared central workspace within arm's reach (0.4 to 0.6 metres) to manipulate a toy assembly on a gridded mat, while the companion faces forward-left and angled downward toward the table rather than looking at the camera wearer. Across the 5 frames, the companion's right hand lifts slightly and moves inward toward the assembly before the camera wearer's right hand enters brightly at the bottom-right in frame 5, partially occluding the companion's left hand and the toy structure, while the companion's lower body and the top of their head remain cropped out of view. Compared to RGB alone, the depth map clearly separates the vertical profile of the open cardboard box and the layered depth ordering of the overlapping hands in frame 5, though it is unreliable for thin flat items like the instruction booklet, small loose blocks on the mat, and fine finger boundaries, which blend smoothly into the table surface.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates a single large pink `person` mask on the right representing the seated companion (about 0.5 to 0.8 metres from the camera wearer), whose torso is angled toward the front-left with head tilted down toward the tabletop rather than toward the camera wearer. Around the tabletop, it detects the instruction manual between the companion's arms (at ~0.5 to 0.6 metres) and stacked items behind the open box (~0.9 to 1.1 metres away, to the left of the person) as `book` masks, while labeling the upright cardboard box at ~0.8 metres on the left in frame 1 as a `handbag`. Everything on the near half of the table—the toy assembly, loose blocks, instruction booklet, and the companion's hands—lies within arm's reach of both the camera wearer and the companion, with the companion's outstretched right arm partially occluding the booklet and table surface behind it and the person's body truncated at the right and top frame edges. Across the 5 frames, the `person` mask shifts its left-reaching contour slightly inward toward the toy structure as the companion's right hand moves from picking up a piece in frames 1–3 to attaching it in frames 4–5, while the camera wearer's right hand enters from the bottom-right in frame 5 and merges into the companion's `person` mask. While the segmentation map makes the silhouette and boundary of the companion's arms against the dark clothing and tabletop easy to trace, it is highly unreliable across time: the cardboard box disappears after frame 1, the camera wearer's left hand is only partially segmented as `remote` in frame 4, the toy assembly and pieces are misclassified as `cell phone` (frame 3) or missed entirely, and a background object on the upper edge is spuriously labeled `potted plant` in frame 4.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks the seated companion on the right (positioned about 0.5 to 0.8 metres from the camera wearer) using yellow body keypoints and magenta hand skeletons against the black background, showing their head cluster at the upper-right tilted downward toward the tabletop rather than facing the camera wearer. In frame 1, only the companion's two magenta hand skeletons are detected in the lower-center foreground (roughly 0.4 to 0.6 metres from the camera wearer and about 0.15 to 0.25 metres apart, with the right hand to the left of and slightly behind the left hand), both well within arm's reach of the camera wearer and the companion. From frames 2 to 5, yellow upper-body linkages appear on the right despite the companion's lower body and right shoulder edge being partly out of view, showing both arms extending forward and to the left over the table as the right hand moves closer to the left hand to join a piece onto the assembly. In frame 5, as the camera wearer's right hand reaches in from the bottom-right at ~0.35 metres and occludes the companion's left hand, the pose estimator swaps tracking onto the camera wearer's larger foreground hand while losing the companion's occluded left hand and right-hand finger details. The pose map reveals exact finger articulation and joint angles of the companion's hands in frames 1 and 2 that are harder to parse in RGB, but it is geometrically unreliable for the torso—missing the body entirely in frame 1 and collapsing the shoulder-hip skeleton into distorted triangles in frames 2, 4, and 5—and fails to separate the camera wearer's hands from the companion's body.
